title: The Purpose of Your Video and Who It Is For
body:
THE BIG IDEA:
Before you record or generate a single second of video, you need one clear answer to this question: who is this video for, and what is the one thing it must do for that person? Think of it like writing a letter. If you sit down to write a letter without knowing who you are sending it to, you will write something vague that helps nobody. A video works the same way. When you know exactly who you are talking to and exactly what problem your video solves, every scene, every word, and every image you create has direction. This lesson teaches you how to find that direction before you waste time building in the wrong place.

STEP-BY-STEP WALKTHROUGH:
Step 1: Name your one viewer. Open the notes app on your phone and write down one sentence that describes your ideal viewer. Be specific. Not "young Nigerians" but "a 22-year-old in Lagos who wants to earn money online but has never made a video before." The more specific your description, the better your video will perform.

Step 2: Identify the one problem your video solves. Write a second sentence that completes this phrase: "After watching my video, my viewer will know how to..." Only one problem per video. If you can list three problems, you have three different videos to make.

Step 3: Choose the right platform for that viewer. TikTok, YouTube Shorts, and Instagram Reels each attract slightly different crowds. If your viewer is a teenager who scrolls TikTok for fun, make it for TikTok. If your viewer is a freelancer searching for how-to answers, YouTube Shorts is the better fit. Write down your chosen platform.

Step 4: Write your video goal in one sentence. Combine your answers into a goal statement like this: "This video teaches a first-time Nigerian creator how to find a niche on TikTok, posted on TikTok, for viewers aged 18 to 25." Keep this note open every time you work on this video.

COMMON MISTAKES TO AVOID:
Mistake 1: Trying to reach everyone. A video made for everyone reaches nobody. The more you narrow your audience, the more that specific audience will feel seen and share your content with others exactly like them.

Mistake 2: Skipping this step and jumping straight to recording. It feels faster to skip the planning, but you will end up remaking the video two or three times. Five minutes of thinking here saves hours of wasted work later.

ONE PRACTICAL TASK FOR TODAY:
Open your phone notes app right now. Write your one viewer sentence, your one problem sentence, and your platform choice. That is your video brief. Keep it. You will use it in every lesson that follows.
takeaway: Know exactly one person and one problem before you create a single second of video.

title: Writing a Short 45-Second Hook-and-Hold Script
body:
THE BIG IDEA:
A 45-second vertical video is not a speech. It is a trap, and a good one. You have three seconds to stop a person from scrolling past, and then you have about 40 more seconds to keep them watching until the end. The way you do this is with a hook-and-hold script. Think of it like fishing. The hook is the shiny thing that makes the fish stop. The hold is the line that keeps pulling the fish in slowly, bit by bit. This lesson teaches you how to write that script using plain language on any free tool.

STEP-BY-STEP WALKTHROUGH:
Step 1: Write your hook sentence. This is the very first line your viewer hears or reads. It must do one of three things: ask a surprising question, make a bold claim, or name a pain point directly. Example: "Most Nigerians making videos online are killing their own reach without knowing it." Write your hook sentence in your notes now.

Step 2: Write three body sentences. Each sentence delivers one piece of useful information that keeps the viewer watching. Think of each sentence as a small promise: you give a little answer, then hint at more. Example sentence 1: "The first mistake is posting without a caption." Example sentence 2: "The second mistake is using the wrong audio." Example sentence 3: "The third mistake is ignoring the first comment."

Step 3: Write your close sentence. This is the final line. It either tells the viewer what to do next (follow, comment, save) or delivers the payoff promise you made at the start. Example: "Fix all three today and watch your numbers change this week." Keep it one sentence.

Step 4: Read it out loud and time it. Open your phone timer. Read your full script at a normal speaking pace. It should take between 40 and 50 seconds. If it is too long, cut one body sentence. If it is too short, expand one body sentence with a specific detail.

COMMON MISTAKES TO AVOID:
Mistake 1: Starting with "Hi, my name is..." Nobody watching a short video cares about your name in the first second. Lead with the problem or the promise, not an introduction.

Mistake 2: Writing like an essay instead of like speech. Read your script out loud before you finalize it. If any sentence sounds odd when spoken, rewrite it in simpler words.

ONE PRACTICAL TASK FOR TODAY:
Using the viewer and problem you wrote in Lesson 1, write a complete 45-second hook-and-hold script right now in your notes app. One hook sentence, three body sentences, one close sentence. Time yourself reading it. Adjust until it lands between 40 and 50 seconds.
takeaway: Hook them in three seconds, then deliver a small promise with every sentence until the end.

title: Storyboarding and Scene Planning
body:
THE BIG IDEA:
A storyboard is a simple plan that shows what the viewer sees and hears at each moment of your video. Think of it like a recipe card for a meal. Before a chef starts cooking, they lay out every ingredient they need and the order they go in. A storyboard does the same thing for your video: it shows each scene, what visual goes in that scene, and what words are spoken at that moment. You do not need to be an artist to make one. You only need a list.

STEP-BY-STEP WALKTHROUGH:
Step 1: Divide your script into scenes. Take the script you wrote in Lesson 2. Each sentence or small group of sentences becomes one scene. A 45-second video will typically have between four and six scenes. Number each scene starting from 1.

Step 2: Describe the visual for each scene. Next to each numbered scene, write one sentence describing what the viewer should see. It does not need to be complicated. Example: "Scene 1: A close-up of a phone screen showing a low-view video." You are not drawing anything. You are only describing.

Step 3: Note any text or caption that appears on screen. If you plan to show a word or phrase on screen during that scene, write it next to the visual description. Example: "Scene 2 visual: a creator looking frustrated at a phone. On-screen text: Mistake 1."

Step 4: Write your full storyboard as a simple table. Use your notes app or a free Google Doc. Make three columns: Scene Number, What the Viewer Sees, What the Viewer Hears. Fill in every row. This becomes your production guide for all the lessons that follow.

COMMON MISTAKES TO AVOID:
Mistake 1: Skipping the storyboard and improvising. Improvising looks spontaneous for experienced creators, but for beginners it produces inconsistent visuals and wasted time generating images that do not fit together.

Mistake 2: Planning too many scenes. A 45-second video does not need eight scenes. Four to six is enough. More scenes means more images to generate and more editing work in CapCut.

ONE PRACTICAL TASK FOR TODAY:
Take your Lesson 2 script and write a simple 4-to-6-scene storyboard right now. Use your notes app. Three columns: Scene, Visual, Audio. Fill every row before moving to Lesson 4.
takeaway: Plan every scene on paper before you generate a single image.

title: Generating Clean Scene Visuals with AI
body:
THE BIG IDEA:
Generating an image with AI is like giving instructions to a very literal assistant who has seen millions of photographs. If you say "a person," you will get something random. If you say "a young Nigerian woman sitting at a wooden desk, looking at a laptop screen, warm indoor lighting, realistic photo style," you will get something close to what you imagined. This lesson teaches you exactly how to write image prompts that give you clean, usable visuals for each scene of your video, using free or low-cost AI image tools.

STEP-BY-STEP WALKTHROUGH:
Step 1: Open a free AI image tool. Go to Leonardo.Ai (leonardo.ai) on your phone browser or laptop and create a free account. It gives you a daily allowance of free image credits. Alternatively, open Adobe Firefly (firefly.adobe.com) which also has a free tier. Do not pay for anything yet.

Step 2: Write a prompt for Scene 1 from your storyboard. Use this format: subject doing action, setting, lighting style, art style. Example: "A young Nigerian man looking at his phone with a confused expression, standing in a small apartment, natural window light, realistic photographic style, vertical crop, 9:16 ratio." Type this into the prompt box and tap Generate.

Step 3: Review and select the best result. Most tools generate four image options at once. Look for the one that is clearest, has no distorted faces or hands, and matches your scene description. Download it to your phone or laptop. If none of the results work, adjust one word in your prompt and generate again.

Step 4: Repeat for each scene in your storyboard. Write a separate prompt for each numbered scene. Download one image per scene. Name each file clearly: scene-1.jpg, scene-2.jpg, and so on. Keep them all in one folder.

COMMON MISTAKES TO AVOID:
Mistake 1: Writing a one-word prompt like "phone." Vague prompts give vague results. The more specific your prompt, the more usable the image.

Mistake 2: Accepting an image with distorted hands or face. AI tools sometimes generate strange fingers or blurry faces. Do not use these. Add "sharp focus, realistic hands" to your prompt, or regenerate until you get a clean result.

ONE PRACTICAL TASK FOR TODAY:
Open Leonardo.Ai right now and generate images for your first two scenes. Download the best result for each. Put them in a folder named "my-video-scenes." You will need them in Lesson 7.
takeaway: Specific prompts produce usable images. Vague prompts waste your credits.

title: Maintaining Visual Consistency Across Scenes
body:
THE BIG IDEA:
Imagine watching a movie where the main character is wearing a red shirt in one scene and a blue shirt in the next scene for no reason. It looks like a mistake and pulls you out of the story. AI-generated images have the same problem: each image is generated fresh, so the character, lighting, and style can change from scene to scene without warning. Visual consistency means making every scene look like it belongs to the same video. This lesson shows you exactly how to control that.

STEP-BY-STEP WALKTHROUGH:
Step 1: Write a "style anchor" sentence and copy it into every prompt. A style anchor is a short phrase that locks the visual style. Example: "realistic photographic style, warm indoor lighting, same Nigerian male character in grey t-shirt, 9:16 vertical frame." Paste this exact phrase at the end of every scene prompt you write.

Step 2: Use the same seed number in Leonardo.Ai. When you generate an image in Leonardo.Ai, you can find a seed number for any result you like. Copy that seed number. When generating the next scene, paste the seed into the seed field. This tells the AI to start from the same visual base, keeping faces and style more consistent.

Step 3: Use Leonardo.Ai's Image Reference feature. Upload your best Scene 1 image as a reference image. Set the influence strength to around 60 to 70 percent. Now generate Scene 2 with your new prompt. The tool will try to match the style and character appearance from Scene 1.

Step 4: Do a visual check before you edit. Line up all your scene images side by side on your phone or laptop. Ask yourself: do the skin tones look similar? Does the lighting feel like the same room or world? If one image stands out badly, regenerate it with your style anchor and reference image active.

COMMON MISTAKES TO AVOID:
Mistake 1: Generating all scenes with different tools. Using Leonardo for Scene 1 and Adobe Firefly for Scene 3 will produce two different visual styles. Pick one tool and use it for all scenes.

Mistake 2: Changing the character description between prompts. If Scene 1 says "young man in grey t-shirt" and Scene 3 says "young man in a shirt," the AI will make different choices. Keep the character description word-for-word identical in every prompt.

ONE PRACTICAL TASK FOR TODAY:
Write your style anchor sentence right now. Then go back to your scene prompts from Lesson 4, add the style anchor to the end of each one, and regenerate any image that does not match. Save all final images in your "my-video-scenes" folder.
takeaway: Lock your style with one anchor phrase and paste it into every single prompt.

title: Generating Natural Voice Narration
body:
THE BIG IDEA:
Your voice narration is the guide that walks the viewer through your video. If the voice sounds robotic or hard to understand, viewers will switch off even if the visuals are good. Think of voice narration like a tour guide at a museum. A good guide sounds warm, clear, and human. A bad guide reads from a script like a machine. AI voice tools have improved so much that many now sound very close to a real human voice. This lesson shows you how to find, test, and use the best free AI voice for your video.

STEP-BY-STEP WALKTHROUGH:
Step 1: Open ElevenLabs or a free alternative. Go to elevenlabs.io on your phone or laptop and create a free account. The free plan gives you enough characters per month for several short videos. If you prefer a fully free option with no sign-up required, go to ttsmp3.com and select a voice there.

Step 2: Paste your script into the text box. Copy the full script you wrote in Lesson 2 and paste it into the text box. Do not paste your storyboard notes. Paste only the words the viewer will hear.

Step 3: Choose the right voice. In ElevenLabs, browse the voice library. Look for voices labeled "conversational" or "narrative." Try at least three voices by tapping the play button next to each. Pick the one that sounds most like a friendly, knowledgeable person. Avoid voices that sound like news announcers or automated systems.

Step 4: Generate and download the audio file. Tap Generate. Listen to the full output. If any word is mispronounced or rushed, go back to your script and add a comma or a period in that spot to slow the AI down. Download the final audio as an MP3 and save it in the same folder as your scene images.

COMMON MISTAKES TO AVOID:
Mistake 1: Using the default voice without testing others. The default voice is rarely the best one. Test at least three before choosing.

Mistake 2: Keeping mispronounced words in the final audio. If the AI mispronounces a word, do not accept it. Try spelling the word phonetically in your script. For example, if "Lagos" sounds wrong, try writing it as "Lay-gos" in the text box to guide the pronunciation.

ONE PRACTICAL TASK FOR TODAY:
Open ElevenLabs right now, paste your Lesson 2 script, test three different voices, and download your final narration audio. Save it as "narration.mp3" in your video folder.
takeaway: Test at least three AI voices before choosing: the right voice keeps viewers listening.

title: Bringing Clips and Voice Together in CapCut
body:
THE BIG IDEA:
CapCut is the editing table where all the pieces you have built in previous lessons come together. Think of it like assembling a jigsaw puzzle. You have your scene images, your narration audio, and your storyboard plan. CapCut is where you lay them all out in order, adjust the timing, and produce a finished video file. CapCut is free, works on Android and iPhone, and is designed exactly for the kind of short vertical videos you are making.

STEP-BY-STEP WALKTHROUGH:
Step 1: Install CapCut and create a new project. Download CapCut from the Google Play Store or Apple App Store if you do not have it already. Open it. Tap "New Project." Select all your scene images in order and tap "Add." CapCut will place them on the timeline automatically.

Step 2: Set each clip duration to match your narration. Tap the first clip on the timeline. Drag the right edge to make it shorter or longer. Your goal is for the total duration of all clips added together to match the total duration of your narration audio. Play your narration file on a separate device or use a timer to know the exact length.

Step 3: Add your narration audio. Tap "Audio" at the bottom of the screen. Tap "Sounds." Then tap "My Device" or "Import." Select your narration.mp3 file. CapCut will place it on the audio track beneath your clips. Drag the audio clip to start at the very beginning of the video. Play the full project and check that the images are changing at a natural pace alongside the words.

Step 4: Adjust clip timing to match what is being said. While the narration plays, watch each scene change. If a scene changes too early or too late compared to the words being spoken about it, tap that clip and drag its edge to fix the timing. The goal is for each visual to match the word or phrase that describes it.

COMMON MISTAKES TO AVOID:
Mistake 1: Adding too many transitions between clips. CapCut has many flashy transition effects. For a professional-looking video, use simple cut or fade transitions only. Too many transitions look amateur and distract from the content.

Mistake 2: Letting one clip run too long with no change. If a single image stays on screen for more than eight seconds with nothing happening, viewers get bored. Break long sections into two images or add a subtle zoom effect in CapCut to keep the eye moving.

ONE PRACTICAL TASK FOR TODAY:
Open CapCut right now. Create a new project with your scene images. Add your narration audio. Adjust clip timings until the visuals and audio feel in sync. Export the video at 1080 by 1920 resolution (CapCut calls this 9:16 format). Save it to your phone.
takeaway: Every image change must feel connected to the word being spoken at that exact moment.

title: Adding Dynamic, Readable Subtitles
body:
THE BIG IDEA:
Most people watch short videos with the sound off, especially in public places. Subtitles are not an afterthought: they are how the majority of your viewers actually read your video. Think of subtitles like the speech bubbles in a comic book. Without them, the reader gets half the story. Good subtitles are large enough to read on a small phone screen, appear word by word or in short phrases, and do not cover important visuals. This lesson shows you how to add clean, readable subtitles inside CapCut without paying for any extra tool.

STEP-BY-STEP WALKTHROUGH:
Step 1: Use CapCut's auto-caption feature. With your project open in CapCut, tap "Text" at the bottom of the screen. Then tap "Auto Captions." CapCut will listen to your narration audio and automatically generate a subtitle track. This takes about 30 seconds for a short video.

Step 2: Check and correct the auto-generated text. CapCut is accurate but not perfect. Tap each caption bubble and read it carefully. Fix any word that was transcribed incorrectly. Pay special attention to Nigerian place names, brand names, or technical terms that may have been mis-heard.

Step 3: Style your subtitles for mobile readability. Tap on a caption and then tap "Style." Set the font to something bold and simple. White text with a thin black outline or shadow is the most readable combination on any background. Set the font size large enough to read without zooming in. Place the subtitles in the lower third of the screen, not at the very bottom where they might be cut off on some phones.

Step 4: Set subtitle animation to word-by-word or karaoke style. In the caption style settings, look for "Animation" or "Effect." Choose "Karaoke" or word-by-word highlight. This makes each word appear or highlight as it is spoken, which keeps viewers reading and watching at the same time.

COMMON MISTAKES TO AVOID:
Mistake 1: Using a small font size. Anything that makes a viewer squint will make them scroll. Make your subtitles bigger than you think they need to be, then test by watching your video on a phone held at arm's length.

Mistake 2: Leaving auto-captions unchecked. Auto-captions are a starting point, not a finished product. Always read through every line before you export.

ONE PRACTICAL TASK FOR TODAY:
Open your CapCut project right now. Tap Auto Captions. Let it generate. Fix every error you find. Set the font to bold white with a black outline. Watch the full video one time before saving.
takeaway: Subtitles are not optional: most of your viewers are watching without sound.

title: Adding Sound Effects and Background Music Responsibly
body:
THE BIG IDEA:
Sound is half the experience of any video, even a short one. The right background music makes a viewer feel energized, focused, or curious. The wrong music makes them close the tab. And if you use a song without the right licence, the platform will mute your video or remove it entirely. Think of music like seasoning on food: a small amount of the right seasoning improves everything, too much destroys the dish, and using something that belongs to someone else without asking gets you thrown out of the kitchen. This lesson shows you exactly where to find safe music and how to use it correctly.

STEP-BY-STEP WALKTHROUGH:
Step 1: Find royalty-free music from a trusted source. Open any of these free, safe libraries in your browser: Pixabay Music (pixabay.com/music), YouTube Audio Library (studio.youtube.com, then click Audio Library), or CapCut's built-in sound library. These tracks are either royalty-free or licensed for use on social platforms. Download one track that matches the mood of your video.

Step 2: Add background music in CapCut. With your project open, tap "Audio," then "Sounds." If you are using CapCut's built-in library, search and add directly. If you downloaded an external track, tap "My Device" and import it. Place the music track on a second audio track beneath your narration.

Step 3: Lower the music volume so it does not compete with the narration. Tap the music track. Find the volume slider. Set the music volume to between 15 and 25 percent. The narration voice must always be clearly louder than the background music. Play the full video to confirm you can hear every word of the narration clearly.

Step 4: Add one or two subtle sound effects at key moments. CapCut has a built-in sound effects library. Search for a soft "whoosh" or "click" sound to accompany a text reveal or a scene change. Tap the moment on the timeline where you want the effect and add it. Keep effects subtle: one or two in a 45-second video is enough.

COMMON MISTAKES TO AVOID:
Mistake 1: Using a popular song from Spotify or Apple Music. These are copyrighted. Using them without a licence will get your video muted, flagged, or removed on YouTube, TikTok, and Instagram. Always use tracks from royalty-free libraries.

Mistake 2: Setting background music at the same volume as your voice. If the viewer has to work to hear the narration over the music, they will leave. Voice first, music second, always.

ONE PRACTICAL TASK FOR TODAY:
Open Pixabay Music right now, pick one track that matches your video mood, download it, and add it to your CapCut project at 20 percent volume. Play the full video and confirm the narration is still clearly heard above the music.
takeaway: Music should be felt, not heard: keep it quiet enough that the voice always wins.

title: Reviewing Rights, Originality, and AI Content Disclosures
body:
THE BIG IDEA:
You have now built a complete AI-assisted video. Before you post it, you need to understand three things: who owns what you created, whether your video is original enough to perform well and to be ethical, and how to disclose that you used AI tools. Think of this like a final quality check before shipping a product. A factory does not ship without inspection, and you should not post without this check either. The good news is that if you followed the steps in this course, you have already done most of the right things. This lesson formalizes it.

STEP-BY-STEP WALKTHROUGH:
Step 1: Check ownership of every asset. Go through your asset list one by one. Your script: you wrote it, you own it. Your AI-generated images: check the terms of the tool you used. Leonardo.Ai and Adobe Firefly grant commercial use on free tiers for user-created outputs. Your AI voice audio: check ElevenLabs terms, as outputs on the free tier are for personal and small creator use. Your background music: confirm it is from Pixabay Music or YouTube Audio Library, which are cleared for social media use. Write a quick checklist and tick each one.

Step 2: Check originality. Ask yourself this honestly: does this video deliver something a real person worked out and shaped, or is it entirely generated without thought? A video where you wrote the script, planned the scenes, chose the visuals, and edited the timing is an original creative work assisted by AI tools. That is acceptable and honest. A video where you typed one sentence and downloaded whatever the AI gave you without any editing or decision-making is not original work. Make sure your video reflects genuine creative decisions.

Step 3: Add an AI disclosure where the platform requires it. YouTube Shorts, TikTok, and Instagram Reels each have policies requiring disclosure when AI was used to create realistic-looking content. On YouTube: when uploading, tick the "Contains AI-generated content" option in the settings panel. On TikTok: add the label "AI-generated content" in your video settings before posting. On Instagram: use the "AI-generated content" label available in advanced settings when posting. Add a brief note in your caption as well, such as: "Visuals created with AI tools."

Step 4: Do a final pre-publish review. Play your complete video one last time. Check that subtitles are correct, music does not overpower the voice, all images are clean with no distorted faces or hands, the script delivers the promise you made in Lesson 1, and your disclosure is in place. If everything passes, export at 1080 by 1920 resolution and post.

COMMON MISTAKES TO AVOID:
Mistake 1: Assuming all AI-generated content is free to use commercially. Each tool has its own terms. Always check the terms of service for every tool you use, especially if you plan to earn money from the video or run it as an advertisement.

Mistake 2: Skipping the disclosure because "everyone does it." Platforms are increasing enforcement of AI disclosure rules. Early compliance builds trust with your audience and protects your account from penalties.

ONE PRACTICAL TASK FOR TODAY:
Before you post your video, complete the four-step checklist above right now. Write it in your notes. Tick each item. Add your AI disclosure on the platform. Then post.
takeaway: Disclose your AI tools, check every asset you own, and only post what you genuinely shaped.
